paper_title: Hidden Messages Between Diffusion Language Model Agents: Causal Evidence for Latent Communication

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Diffusion language models form answers through a sequence of revisable continuous states, but multi-agent systems usually discard those states and make agents communicate only after decoding text. We ask whether one independent diffusion trajectory can pass a compact hidden message into another and, crucially, whether the receiver uses what that message means. In Hidden Messages, a sender compresses its denoising state into four signed dense vectors; the receiver consumes them while retaining its own context, canvas, and trajectory. Removing a message tests whether the channel matters; replacing it with a message from another example tests whether its content matters. Across controlled tasks, derangement removes a +63.6-point advantage on Tiny-A2D and a +100.0-point advantage on Dream-7B, while targeted substitutions steer the receiver toward the substituted fact. On QASC with the two supporting facts split across agents, matched communication reaches 80.8%, but a wrong-example message lowers accuracy to 46.8%, a content effect of +34.0 points. The surprising result is temporal: one late transfer reaches 87.8%, exceeding four recurrent exchanges by +7.0 points. These experiments provide causal evidence for continuous hidden communication between diffusion-LM agents and show that when information is transferred can matter more than how many times agents exchange it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Masked diffusion language models generate by repeatedly revising partially masked sequence rather than committing to left-to-right token stream [Li et al., 2022, Sahoo et al., 2024, Nie et al., 2025, Ye et al., 2025, Zhou et al., 2026]. Between the initial mask and the final answer lies rich sequence of continuous states. single model uses those states internally, then throws them away. group of agents could instead treat them as communication surface. Imagine two agents looking at different pieces of the same problem. One knows which fact is needed; the other holds table containing that fact. text-only protocol makes the first agent finish sentence before the second can use the request. hidden-state protocol can hand over compact continuous representation while both answers are still being revised. This is the object we study: messages between independent diffusion-LM agents, with no shared canvas, context, token prediction, or trajectory. Recent latent multi-agent systems relay hidden states or keyvalue caches between autoregressive models [Du et al., 2026, Zou et al., 2026], while other work preserves state within one Accepted at the DiffuLM Workshop at NeurIPS 2026. diffusion model or transfers partially denoised sequences [Xia et al., 2026, Rozonoyer et al., 2026, Yun et al., 2026]. Here the boundary is agent-to-agent and continuous, but each denoising process remains its own. We train task-specific communication adapter with supervision around frozen backbones: the question is whether this learned channel carries causally useful content, not whether communication protocol emerges without supervision. An accuracy increase alone, however, is not evidence that hidden message conveys the senders example-specific content. The receiver could benefit from generic activation, extra compute, or distributional cue. Causal audits of latent channels have made this distinction explicit for autoregressive agents [Zhang and Emu, 2026, Cheng et al., 2026]. We bring this standard to diffusionLM collaboration: the message entering the receiver is replaced while everything else is held fixed. matched message is compared both with no message and with deranged message produced for another example. The first contrast asks whether the channel matters; the second asks whether the receiver uses the right content. We follow the idea from its smallest causal test to natural reasoning task. Tiny-A2D asks whether compact diffusion backbone can learn an example-specific channel at all. The Dream-7B dependencyspanning task then asks whether the same causal signature survives scale and dependency that requires information to travel out and back. Finally, distributed QASC asks whether the channel changes answers when scientific evidence is split across agents. This progression exposes result that simple more interaction is better comparison would miss: repeated exchange is indispensable for the out-and-back dependency, yet one late transfer beats four recurrent exchanges on QASC. The relevant design variable is not raw round count but the match between tasks dependency structure and the moment at which hidden state becomes useful. Our contributions are threefold: We introduce supervised signed dense message channel for diffusion-LM agents and instantiate it on Tiny-A2D and Dream-7B while preserving independent contexts, canvases, random-number streams, and denoising trajectories. We establish content-sensitive communication through receiver-side interventions: removing, deranging, zeroing, randomizing, or self-substituting messages while retaining fixed designated receiver. We identify temporal principle across three empirical settings: recurrent communication helps when dependencies are sequential, whereas late fusion can be both simpler and more accurate when private evidence is independently computable. Code and artifacts: https://github.com/alanrbtx/hidden-messages-diffusion-agents

sections.title: 2 Related work
sections.content: Latent multi-agent communication. Interlat learns compressed hidden-state communication between language-model agents [Du et al., 2026]; LatentMAS relays latent thoughts through shared working memory [Zou et al., 2026]; and Latent-DARM bridges diffusion planners and autoregressive executors [Berrayana et al., 2026]. These works establish that text is not the only viable agent interface. Our focus is the denoising-time interface between diffusion-LM agents and the causal identity of compact message, with independent rather than shared canvases. This distinction turns communication into testable object: the sender-side message can be replaced without replacing the receivers context or trajectory. State across diffusion steps. MetaState and Relay preserve continuous computation across successive passes of one diffusion model [Xia et al., 2026, Rozonoyer et al., 2026]. TIE transfers promising partially denoised sequences across models [Yun et al., 2026]. HIDDEN MESSAGES instead transports compressed hidden message between separate agents; the receiving canvas itself is never replaced. This distinction is important for attributing an effect to communication rather than trajectory selection. Causal audits. Recent audits show that message presence, example-specific content, and sender identity are separate properties of latent channels [Zhang and Emu, 2026, Cheng et al., 2026]. sections.title: 3 Hidden communication between diffusion agents
sections.content: 3.1 Independent trajectories and continuous interface Consider agents {0, . . . , 1}. Agent has private context ci, masked canvas xt i, and its own denoising trajectory. At an exchange point t, an encoder reads the task-relevant part of hidden state ht and produces compact message = Eθ(ht zt i) RKd, (1) The transmitted object is signed BF16 tensor, not token IDs, class probabilities, logits, or partially decoded sequence. Incoming messages from other agents are averaged and decoded into receiver-side conditioning state, = 4, = 128. zt = 1 1 zt j, (cid:88) j=i = Dϕ(zt rt i). (2) On Tiny-A2D, Eθ attends over the sender token states and Dϕ fuses the decoded message into the receivers answer state through gated residual. On Dream-7B, the encoder reads the answer-position state and the decoder produces virtual prefix embeddings, RMS-matched to the backbone input embeddings and prepended to the receivers next pass. In recurrent exchange the prefix persists until it is replaced. No agent sees another agents text context or canvas. 3.2 Supervised task-specific channel adaptation The channel is lightweight, task-specific adapter comprising message encoder and receiver-side fusion or projection module. The backbone and language-model head are frozen in every reported channel experiment; supervision trains the communication interface rather than the diffusion models. For Tiny-A2D, the compressor and residual fuser are learned jointly: union-context hidden states act as teacher, while paired matched-versus-deranged supervision makes messages discriminate between counterfactual sender facts. For Dream-7B [Ye et al., 2025], an auxiliary classifier first encourages the message to preserve the requested slot, returned code, or QASC answer label; variance term prevents collapse. We then freeze the encoder and align the receiver-side projector to short answer-oriented prefix embeddings using cosine and relative mean-squared error. Supervision shapes the message geometry, but neither the label, teacher context, nor any text message is available to the receiver at inference time. The reported settings use task-specific channel training, not single universal adapter transferred across all tasks. Exact optimization settings are given in Appendix A. 3 3.3 Causal and temporal interventions Let (x, z) indicate whether the designated receiver answers example correctly under message input z. We evaluate three core interventions: presence = E[Y (x, z(x)) (x, )], content = E[Y (x, z(x)) (x, z(π(x)))], (3) (4) where π is deterministic permutation to different-target example whenever possible. Because the receiver input, local trajectory, and evaluation item are unchanged, the second contrast attributes the difference to message identity rather than mere channel presence. We also compare recurrent delivery with late-only delivery: agents first process private evidence independently, then exchange once immediately before the receiver decision. Zero, moment-matched random, and self-message replacements serve as additional checks (Appendix B).

sections.title: 4 Experimental setup
sections.content: 4.1 Two backbones, three views of the channel HM-Synth Chain on Tiny-A2D. We begin with the minimal causal question: can information cross the hidden boundary at all? HM-Synth generates chains of two to four lookup facts and splits them across two private contexts. Each counterfactual pair keeps the designated receivers context fixed but changes sender-side fact and therefore the correct answer. The frozen Tiny-A2D backbone sees 10,000 training examples and no union context at inference; only 6.1 MiB communication module is learned. We evaluate 1,000 counterfactual pairs (2,000 examples), making both message derangement and targeted fact replacement unambiguous. This benchmark acts as microscope for the channel: when the receiver input is fixed and only the sender fact changes, corresponding answer change has only one route across the agent boundary. Dream-7B dependency spanning. Agent 0 knows which of ten slots is requested but does not have the code table. Agent 1 has the complete, randomly ordered table but is not told which slot is requested. Solving the task requires two-stage out-and-back exchange: agent 0 communicates the requested slot, agent 1 uses that message to select the relevant code, and agent 1 communicates the code back before agent 0 commits its answer. We evaluate 512 counterfactual pairs (1,024 examples) with disjoint private contexts. In addition to example derangement, wrong-fact intervention swaps table entry while preserving agent 0s context; this lets us test whether the final prediction follows the substituted content. The first transfer is therefore query and the second reply; single late handoff cannot recover the intermediate computation that never took place. Distributed QASC. QASC questions are annotated with two facts whose composition supports an eight-way answer [Khot et al., 2020]. We give one gold fact to each of two agents, add four disjoint leakage-filtered distractors per agent, and keep the question and options common. Neither agent sees the others evidence. The channel is learned only from the 7,134 derived training examples and evaluated on all 1,000 derived development examples. Agent 0 is fixed as receiver in every condition; there is no voting or logit averaging. This setting replaces synthetic codes with ordinary scientific statements while preserving the central information constraint: the scored receiver must combine evidence that it never observes in one text context. Inference and uncertainty. For QASC, recurrent communication consists of four synchronous exchanges followed by one receiver decision; late-only communication consists of one independent pass per agent, one exchange, and the same receiver decision. We reuse identical item order and receiver inputs across conditions. HM-Synth and QASC accuracy contrasts use 5,000 and 10,000 paired bootstrap resamples over examples, respectively, with percentile 95% intervals. The Dream-7B dependency-spanning row in Table 1 reports the aggregate over locked evaluations; its item-level causal contrasts have the same direction throughout. Table 1: Three views of the hidden channel. Accuracies are percentages and contrasts are percentage points. Tiny-A2D establishes content transfer on HM-Synth; the Dream-7B dependency-spanning task tests sequential dependency, and distributed QASC tests split natural evidence. The schedule reversal in the last column is the central timing result: late fusion fails on the Dream-7B dependencyspanning task but wins on QASC. Setting No msg. Matched Deranged Late Match.der. sections.title: 5 Results
sections.content: 5.1 The receiver follows the message, not merely the channel Tiny-A2D supplies the first causal trace. matched message raises HM-Synth accuracy from 8.6% to 72.9%; message from different-target example returns performance to 9.3%. The matchedminus-deranged effect is +63.6 points with 95% paired bootstrap CI [+61.5, +65.8], while random, zero, and self messages all remain near chance. More revealingly, when we replace the senders fact, the receiver changes its answer in 89.4% of examples and selects the substituted target in 72.9%. The vector is therefore carrying decision-relevant fact, not merely opening learned gate. The Dream-7B dependency-spanning task reproduces the same signature in harder out-and-back exchange. Matched two-stage communication reaches 100.0%, compared with 9.8% without message and 0.0% under derangement. Swapping the table fact steers the receiver to the replacement target in 100.0% of examples. Scaling the backbone does not wash out the causal dependence on message identity; it sharpens it. The same causal signature appears on natural questions. QASC accuracy rises from 72.6% without communication to 80.8% with matched recurrent messages. The +8.2-point paired gain has interval [+5.7, +10.7]. More decisively, replacing each message with one produced for different-target question reduces accuracy to 46.8%: the matched-minus-deranged content effect is +34.0 points with interval [+30.7, +37.2]. Wrong content is substantially worse than silence. channel whose benefit came only from additional computation or constant learned prefix would not be sensitive to which question produced the message, much less be harmed by receiving the wrong one. 5.2 The right moment beats more rounds The direction of the schedule effect reverses with the information structure. The Dream-7B dependency-spanning task needs messages at two different points: agent 1 cannot select the requested code before receiving the slot identity. Recurrent exchange reaches 100.0%, but one late message reaches only 10.8%, near the no-communication level. The first message is useful not because it contains the final answer, but because it changes what the other agent computes next. QASC has different structure. Each agent can interpret its own supporting fact before any exchange. Here, single late transfer reaches 87.8%, outperforming the four-round recurrent schedule by +7.0 points ([+4.4, +9.6]). The late schedule transmits only once and uses three agent forward passes, compared with four transmissions and nine forward passes for the recurrent schedule, yet it is more accurate. Repeatedly injecting provisional states appears to interfere with independent evidence formation; delaying fusion lets the sender first form more decision-ready representation. The two regimes suggest temporal design rule. If one agents next computation is conditional on anothers partial result, the message must arrive early enough to redirect that computation. If private evidence can mature independently, early repeated fusion can be counterproductive and the best handoff is close to the decision. Round count is therefore poor proxy for collaboration depth: the useful quantity is whether the exchange point aligns with the tasks latent dependency graph.

sections.title: 6 Discussion
sections.content: What travels through the channel. Matched accuracy alone would leave the mechanism ambiguous: learned prefix might simply make the receiver more confident or place it in generally favorable activation regime. The replacement experiments tell more specific story. Messages produced for the wrong example hurt, while targeted fact substitutions redirect the receiver toward the substituted answer. We therefore do not need to translate the vectors into sentences to test whether they carry decision-relevant content; changing their origin while holding the receiver fixed changes the decision in predictable direction. This supports hidden communication, not claim of human-readable or emergent language. Communication has clock. The schedule reversal shows why an agent protocol cannot be summarized by its round count. In the Dream-7B dependency-spanning task, the first message determines what the other agent should compute, so waiting until the end removes the opportunity to perform that computation. In QASC, each agent can first form useful representation of its own evidence, and early repeated fusion can disturb that process. Both settings use the same Dream-7B backbone, so the reversal is not trivial consequence of comparing different model sizes; it is consistent with the dependency structure and the point at which message becomes actionable. The broader design opportunity is an adaptive protocol that exchanges when latent dependency is ready, rather than on fixed clock.

sections.title: 7 Limitations and future work
sections.content: The controlled evidence spans Tiny-A2D and Dream-7B, but natural-question evidence currently comes from Dream-7B on QASC; larger teams, other diffusion backbones, and long-form generation may produce different channel geometries. The channels are supervised, task-specific adapters, so the results establish learned hidden communication but not an emergent language or taskindependent protocol. Initial zero-shot reuse across heterogeneous tasks did not yield detectable benefit. Applying the channel to new task may therefore require new supervision and adapter retraining or explicit cross-domain alignment; successful zero-shot transfer is not established by these experiments. Matched text-channel and wall-clock comparisons are also future work. Finally, latent channel is not privacy mechanism: dense states may encode sensitive information even when they are not human-readable. particularly consequential next setting is multi-agent code generation with deliberately partitioned context: different agents may see the specification, relevant source files, tests, or execution feedback. Continuous hidden communication could carry task-specific intermediate state across these boundaries without requiring every exchange to be verbalized, while matchedversus-deranged interventions would test whether successful code changes causally depend on the transmitted content. This setting also sharpens the timing question: message should arrive when cross-agent dependency becomes actionable, rather than at every decoding round. We therefore view context-partitioned software engineering, together with content-dependent message policy, as the primary direction for scaling the method.

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: With supervised task-specific adapter, diffusion-LM agents can exchange useful information without verbalizing it. From Tiny-A2D HM-Synth to the Dream-7B dependency-spanning task and distributed QASC, removing, deranging, or surgically replacing the hidden message changes fixed receiver in the predicted direction. That sequence of interventions is the causal evidence: example-specific content crosses the latent boundary. The central result is not that more messages are always better. Two-stage exchange is essential when one agents computation depends on anothers earlier message, while single late transfer is superior when private evidence can mature independently. Hidden communication is therefore temporal coordination problem: the moment of transfer can matter more than the number of rounds.

sections.title: A Implementation and evaluation details
sections.content: We use the Tiny-A2D checkpoint dllm-hub/Qwen3-0.6B-diffusion-mdlm-v0.1 [Zhou et al., 2026] and Dream-v0-Instruct-7B, both with BF16 weights. Dream uses SDPA attention, and both model checkpoints are released under Apache-2.0. QASC is used under CC-BY-4.0. Exact pinned model and dataset revisions are recorded with the released configurations rather than in the paper prose. The derived QASC split contains 7,134 training, 1,000 development, and 926 held-out examples; this paper reports the full development set and does not select examples by method output. HM-Synth contains 5,000 training, 500 validation, and 1,000 test counterfactual pairs, with disjoint generator ranges and two to four hops. The Tiny-A2D channel has four 128-dimensional slots and width 256. Its 960-step AdamW run uses batch size 64, learning rate 3 104, weight decay 102, union-teacher weight 0.5, and paired-separation weight 0.2 on one quarter of each batch. Only split private contexts are available at evaluation. The Dream encoder is LayerNormLinearSiLULinear with per-slot LayerNorm; its LinearSiLU Linear prefix projector is RMS-calibrated to input embeddings. Representation learning combines answer-class cross-entropy with feature-variance penalty (weight 0.1, target standard deviation 0.2); prefix alignment uses cosine distance plus 0.25 relative MSE. Both stages use AdamW for 1,000 steps, batch size 128, learning rate 103, weight decay 104, gradient clipping at 1.0, and 5% warmup. Code and artifacts. The implementation, exact configurations and revisions, learned channel weights, per-example predictions, and table-generation code are available at https://github.com/ alanrbtx/hidden-messages-diffusion-agents. Tiny-A2D used an NVIDIA Quadro RTX 8000 with CUDA 13.0 and PyTorch 2.12 for 1,293.3 seconds (0.36 GPU-hours). Dream used NVIDIA H100 80GB GPUs with the same stack: QASC evaluation took 754.6 seconds (0.21 GPU-hours), and controlled channel training plus evaluation took 8,988.7 seconds (2.50 GPU-hours). These totals exclude download, artifact verification, and other runs.

sections.title: B Intervention details
sections.content: Deranged message. The sender message is permuted across evaluation rows while the receivers prompt, private context, and target stay fixed. For QASC, the permutation is constrained to different answer label. For the controlled task, counterfactual pairs and different-slot batches ensure that both fact and slot replacements are defined. Zero, random, and self controls. The zero condition replaces every message element with zero. The random condition samples tensor with the empirical first and second moments of the matched messages at that round. The self condition injects an agents own message through the same projection 8 path. These conditions help separate task content from vector presence, magnitude, and receiver-side activation. Integrity. Every agent receives separate token row and maintains its own diffusion state. Communication-off predictions are exactly identical to the unmodified backbone path. The primary output is always agent 0; no vote, canvas replacement, logit averaging, or union-context oracle is used. Paired bootstrap intervals resample evaluation rows with replacement and recompute the accuracy difference for 10,000 replicates.
